title: Deduplicating Training Data Makes LMs Better
hook: Training corpora are full of copies — one 61-word sentence shows up 60,000+ times in C4. Strip the duplicates and models memorize far less and evaluate more honestly.
key_points: Corpora hold many near-duplicates; one 61-word sentence appears 60,000+ times in C4.
Deduplication cuts verbatim memorized output by roughly 10x.
It reduces train-test overlap, which affected about 4% of validation examples.
Less overlap enables more accurate evaluation.
content_html: Katherine Lee, Daphne Ippolito, Andrew Nystrom, and colleagues found that language-model training corpora contain many near-duplicate examples and repeated substrings — strikingly, one 61-word sentence appears over 60,000 times in the C4 dataset. They show that cleaning this up changes how models behave.
extra_html:
How it works

After deduplicating the data, the authors measure roughly a 10x reduction in verbatim memorized output, meaning the model regurgitates training text far less often. Deduplication also improves training efficiency and cuts down train-test overlap, which they find had contaminated about 4% of validation examples.

Why it matters

Less overlap between training and test data enables more accurate evaluation, since a model can no longer score well simply by having seen the answers. Together with the drop in memorization, the work makes a practical case that careful data hygiene is a cheap, high-leverage step before training a language model.

related.title: The Pile: 800GB of Diverse Text
related.hook: Web text alone leaves gaps. The Pile stitches together 22 curated sources — academic and professional — so a language model picks up knowledge plain web crawls miss.

related.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
related.hook: Loss doesn't drop randomly as models grow — it follows a smooth power law in size, data, and compute. That predictability is what made betting on bigger models rational.
